I have gathered extensive material. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes from what I have from all the sources. Here are the notes:

# 1 Samuel 29 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records how God providentially delivered David from fighting alongside the Philistines against Israel. David, having fled to Philistine territory in a time of discouragement (1 Samuel 27), now finds himself marching with the Philistine army against his own people. The Philistine commanders object to his presence, and Achish reluctantly sends him home — sparing David from the impossible dilemma of either fighting against Israel or betraying Achish.

**Key Outline (from Ellicott):** David and his band are looked upon by the Philistine lords with suspicion and obliged to withdraw, while preserving the friendship of Achish. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

**Dr. Constable** notes that this chapter seems to antedate chapter 28 slightly; the writer may have placed it here to highlight the contrasts between Saul and David in chapters 27–31. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-29.html

---

## v. 1 — The Armies Gather

> "Now the Philistines brought all their forces together at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel."

- **Aphek:** The name means "a fort or strong place" and was common for several "places of arms" in Canaan. This Aphek was most likely in the Plain of Jezreel; Eusebius placed it near En-dor. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill:** Aphek here was not the one in Judah (1 Sam 4:1) but rather in the tribe of Asher (Josh 19:30), unless there was one in Issachar near Jezreel and Shunem. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **The spring/fountain in Jezreel:** Identified by modern travellers as *Ain-Jalûd*, the "Fountain of Goliath," a large spring flowing from under a cavern in the rock at the base of Mount Gilboa. Robinson called it "the ancient fountain of Jezreel, where Saul and Jonathan pitched before their last fatal battle." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Precept Austin:** "Now" marks the writer returning to the story from 1 Sam 28:4 after the interruption of Saul's visit to the medium. Jezreel means "God Scatters," which is exactly what happened to Israel's forces. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary

- **Guzik:** The battle lines were drawn from the previous chapter; the Philistines intended to deliver a death-blow to Israel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

---

## v. 2 — David Marches in the Rear

> "As the Philistine leaders marched out their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men marched behind them with Achish."

- **Ellicott:** The "lords" are a different term from "princes." In the Philistine federation there were five sovereign princes (of whom Achish of Gath was one), and beneath them other chieftains who had great control. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill:** The lords marched some at the head of hundreds, others at the head of thousands. Achish as generalissimo brought up the rear, and David (whom Achish had appointed captain of his bodyguard, 1 Sam 28:2) attended him with his men. David could not refuse out of gratitude, yet was in the greatest strait — waiting and hoping for Providence to deliver him. Gill notes that the Jewish commentator Abarbinel thought David only intended to be Achish's bodyguard, not to actually fight against Israel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** David is among the Philistines because in his discouragement he left the people of God and the land of Israel (1 Sam 27). He now finds himself among the ungodly, ready to fight against God's people. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Precept Austin:** David was about to be gored by one of the "horns of his dilemma" — fight against his own people, or tell Achish he could not. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary

---

## v. 3 — The Commanders Question David's Presence

> "Then the commanders of the Philistines asked, 'What about these Hebrews?' Achish replied, 'Is this not David, the servant of King Saul of Israel? He has been with me all these days, even years, and from the day he defected until today I have found no fault in him.'"

- **"What are these Hebrews doing here?"** — The Philistine leaders looked at David and his men and understood they didn't belong. They were Hebrews who worshiped another God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **F.B. Meyer (quoted by Precept Austin and Enduring Word):** "It is very terrible when the children of the world have a higher sense of Christian propriety and fitness than Christians themselves, and say to one another, 'What do these Hebrews here?'" The word "Hebrew" means "one who has passed over" — a separatist. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Guzik:** The Philistine leaders could see what David was blind to — David had started to think and act like a Philistine and was ready to fight against God's people. They knew who David really was even when David forgot. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Gill:** Achish exaggerated "these years" — David had been with him only one year and four months (1 Sam 27:7), though "strictly speaking he was not incorrect." David had successfully deceived Achish for 16 months. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary

- **A sobering testimony:** It is a sad thing that a Philistine ruler defended David so confidently. Achish knew he "had David in his pocket." Hearing "David has been with me," "I have found no fault in him," and "he defected to me" should have grieved David profoundly. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Ellicott:** "These days, or these years" is an indefinite expression of time. The Syriac renders it "this time, and time, and months." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

---

## v. 4 — The Commanders Demand David Be Sent Away

> "But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with Achish and told him, 'Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not go down with us into battle only to become our adversary during the war. What better way for him to regain the favor of his master than with the heads of our men?'"

- **Gill:** They spoke of David with contempt — "this fellow." They did not wish him sent to Saul (lest reconciliation strengthen Israel), but back to Ziklag. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Ellicott:** "Go down" is a technical military expression — troops descended from hill country to the plain for battle. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Treasury of Scripture Knowledge (via Precept Austin):** "The princes reasoned wisely… it was ordered by a gracious Providence that they refused to let David go… Had he fought for the Philistines, he would have fought against God and his country; and had he in the battle gone over to the Israelites, he would have deceived and become a traitor to the hospitable Achish. God therefore delivered him from such disgrace." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary

- **Providence:** Precept Austin notes Proverbs 21:1 — "The king's heart is like channels of water in the hand of the LORD; He turns it wherever He wishes." God moved the hearts of the Philistine commanders. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "It must be considered a happy circumstance in the overruling providence of God to rescue David out of the dangerous dilemma in which he was now placed." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/1-samuel-29.html

- **G. Campbell Morgan (via Precept Austin):** "Here, then, along the line of perfectly natural emotions, God is seen acting on behalf of His servant. He made the wrath of the princes praise Him, in that it accomplished His purpose." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary

---

## v. 5 — They Remember the Victory Song

> "'Is this not the David about whom they sing in their dances: "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands"?'"

- **Gill:** The song that originally excited Saul's jealousy (1 Sam 18:7) was also current among the Philistines. The more valiant and victorious David had been against them, the less he could be trusted. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** The faith-filled victory over Goliath seemed like a distant memory for a backslidden David, but the Philistines remembered it well. The song of David's victory came back to haunt him again. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Ellicott:** The folk-songs were known among the Philistines, who seem to have been a musical people. David's learning Philistine music in Gath and later introducing it into Jerusalem has been noted by scholars. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

---

## v. 6 — Achish Tells David He Must Go

> "So Achish summoned David and told him, 'As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright in my sight, and it seems right that you should march in and out with me in the army, because I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until this day. But you have no favor in the sight of the leaders.'"

- **"As the LORD lives":** This is unexpected in a Philistine oath. Baldwin (cited by Guzik) suggests Achish may have been courteous to David by not swearing by Philistine gods. Keil (cited by Ellicott) similarly thinks Achish used the formula most acceptable to David. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill:** Though a heathen, Achish may have had some knowledge of the true God from his conversation with David, or used the name out of complaisance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **David's "uprightness":** Gill observes that David was not as sincere as Achish thought — he had lied about his raids (1 Sam 27:10–12). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** David thought he couldn't be at peace in Israel (1 Sam 27:1). Now his "Philistine friends" won't accept him either. He has no home — trying to live in both worlds leaves him homeless in both. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **"Worst place for any child of God":** David had too much of the world in him to be at peace in the LORD, and too much of the LORD in him to be at peace in the world. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Constable** notes the parallel with Pilate's threefold vindication of Jesus (John 18:38; 19:4, 6): here Achish vindicates David three times (vv. 3, 6, 9). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-29.html

---

## v. 7 — "Go in Peace"

> "'Therefore turn back now and go in peace, so that you will not do anything to displease the leaders of the Philistines.'"

- **"Go in peace":** Gill notes the Jewish rabbis distinguish between wishing someone to "go in peace" (which they say has not issued happily) versus "go to peace" (which has). They cite Jethro to Moses and David to Absalom as examples of the former. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** David used to displease the lords of the Philistines all the time as a mighty warrior for God. Now he is concerned about *not* displeasing them — a mark of his backsliding. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **God's use of rejection:** Guzik notes that many hesitate to live fully for Christ because they fear the rejection of the ungodly. But God can use that rejection for good. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

---

## v. 8 — David's Protest

> "'But what have I done?' David replied. 'What have you found against your servant, from the day I came to you until today, to keep me from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king?'"

- **A difficult verse:** This is the most debated verse in the chapter. David seems to protest being dismissed from fighting against Israel.

- **Ellicott:** "David's words have a ring of falseness in them; he never contemplated fighting in the ranks against Israel, and yet he speaks thus. The generous confidence of the chivalrous Achish is here in painful contrast with the dissimulation of the Israelite chieftain, David." Ellicott also notes the suggestion that David deliberately aroused suspicions to bring about his dismissal — this is possible, given the embarrassing situation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill:** David's question "cannot be excused of great dissimulation, since nothing was more foreign from his heart, and against his will, than fighting against the Israelites." David was "glad at heart" to be excused but put on these airs so the Philistines would have no cause for suspicion while he continued living among them. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** David seems genuinely disappointed that he will not be able to fight for the Philistines against Israel. His heart was in a bad place, but God didn't abandon him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **"My lord the king":** A debated phrase. **Constable** thinks David probably wanted Achish to think he meant Achish, but David really meant Saul — continuing his deception. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-29.html

- **Grant's Commentary:** David does not expressly speak of fighting against the enemies of *Achish*, but against those of "my lord the king." Achish assumed David meant him, but David still considered Saul his lord. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-samuel-29.html

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "David is not free from censure in his professions to Achish, to do what he probably had not the smallest purpose of doing… It is just an instance of the unhappy consequences into which a false step — a departure from the straight course of duty — will betray everyone who commits it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "There is enough ambiguity in his words… to indicate David's continued deception of Achish, and perhaps to actually turn on him in the ensuing battle just as the lords feared." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-29.html

---

## v. 9 — "As an Angel of God"

> "Achish replied, 'I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God. But the commanders of the Philistines have said, "He must not go into battle with us."'"

- **"As an angel of God":** Ellicott calls this a simile Achish most likely borrowed from Hebrew thought, used in graceful courtesy as something acceptable to David. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill:** Achish meant it for David's great wisdom, graceful behaviour, and inoffensive carriage. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Gill adds:** Though Achish was one of the five lords, the other four outvoted him, so he was obliged to submit. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary (Blaikie):** "The only bright spot in this transaction was the very cordial testimony borne by Achish… It is seldom indeed that such language as Achish employed can be used of any servant… David had shown that singular, unblemished trustworthiness that earned such golden opinions for Joseph in the house of Potiphar." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Kingcomments** (more critical): Achish "even sees David as a messenger from God. As an idolater he can only mean that he sees a good spirit in David. David has so much surrendered his true identity… because of his life in the lie, that he has given Achish a false image of what a messenger of God is." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-samuel-29.html

- **Constable** notes this is the third time Achish vindicates David, paralleling Pilate's threefold vindication of Jesus. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-29.html

---

## v. 10 — Ordered to Depart at Dawn

> "'Now then, get up early in the morning, along with your master's servants who came with you, and go as soon as it is light.'"

- **"Your master's servants":** This is a perplexing phrase. Ellicott says it is "hardly the expression we should expect Achish to use of David's followers." Ellicott suggests it may refer to men from Manasseh who had only recently defected to David (1 Chronicles 12:19–21) and may have been known to some Philistines as Saul's soldiers — perhaps their presence had first awakened the Philistine suspicions. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill:** The phrase "tacitly carried in it the objection of the Philistine lords" — since the men were servants of Saul, they could not be trusted in battle against him, lest they seize an opportunity to regain Saul's favour. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Achish's urgency:** Gill says Achish advised them to get away as soon as possible, lest the Philistines fall upon them. This pressing charge to leave at first light providentially got David back to Ziklag in time to rescue the captives taken by the Amalekites (chapter 30). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** David wanted to fight with the Philistines against Israel, but God wouldn't let him. David's heart was in a bad place, but God didn't abandon him. We should praise God for the times He keeps us from sinning as badly as we might want to. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

---

## v. 11 — David Returns; The Philistines Advance

> "So David and his men got up early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. And the Philistines went up to Jezreel."

- **Gill:** David and his men were "as willing and ready to go as the Philistines were desirous they should." Ziklag was within the principality of Gath, perhaps 88 miles away (per Bunting), though Gill doubts it was that far. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Ellicott:** "No doubt David and his officers rejoiced at their escaping the terrible alternative of either turning traitors to the kindly man who had so hospitably received them… or of appearing in arms with the Philistines when they came into collision with the Israelites under Saul. But they little thought in how sore a danger their wives and children and homes were at this juncture. Their release from the Philistine army was not a moment too soon to save these." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

- **Gill on Providence:** "By the dismission of David… he was not only delivered from a sad plight… but also, by the pressing charge of Achish to get away as early as possible in the morning, he came time enough to rescue the prey the Amalekites had taken at Ziklag." Additionally, had David stayed in the Philistine camp, "it would not have been so easy for him, on the death of Saul, to have got from them, and succeed in the kingdom, as he could and did from Ziklag." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

- **Guzik:** David returned "to the land of the Philistines" — not yet back to Israel. The Holy Spirit made all these events a wake-up call, but David didn't yet hear it. It would take a dramatic crisis (chapter 30) to bring him back. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

- **Kingcomments:** "While Saul has disappeared forever in the night, the new morning is dawning for David." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-samuel-29.html

---

## Traditions: Points of Difference

### Reformed / Presbyterian

From **Ligonier Ministries** (R.C. Sproul's ministry), the treatment of David's actions in chapters 27–29 is notably cautious: "It is hard to know how to evaluate David's actions… If they were sinful, let us note that David still accomplished good for Israel by defeating many of the nation's enemies. Sometimes we put ourselves in certain difficult situations because of our sin, but that does not mean God cannot bring about good." The Reformed emphasis is on God's sovereignty in using even David's failures providentially. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-deceives-achish

### Baptist

**Gill (Calvinistic Baptist):** Gill is blunt about David's sin — calling his words in v. 8 "great dissimulation" that "cannot be excused." He emphasizes God's meticulous providence: the dismissal not only saved David from the immediate dilemma but also positioned him perfectly to rescue Ziklag and, after Saul's death, to ascend the throne from Ziklag rather than from a Philistine war camp. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-29.html

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Emphasizes three lessons: (1) Leading a double life will finally result in distrust and discovery; (2) God is faithful to extricate His children and bring to pass His will even when they go astray; (3) God's people will recognize His rightful leaders and rally to their aid. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-29.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

**Enduring Word (David Guzik):** The emphasis is strongly applicational — David as a warning about "trying to straddle two worlds." Guzik sees David as genuinely backslidden and willing to fight against Israel, making God's intervention an act of pure mercy to keep him from sin he wanted to commit. The tone is pastoral and devotional. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-29/

### Anglican

**Ellicott:** Takes a moderately critical view of David's dissimulation but allows the possibility that David deliberately provoked the suspicions to engineer his own dismissal. Ellicott pays careful attention to geography, textual variants (LXX), and military terminology. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/29.htm

### Methodist / Holiness

**Clarke's Commentary:** Adam Clarke states clearly: "Had he gone, he had his choice of two sins… God, therefore, so ordered it in his mercy that he was not permitted to go to a battle in which he was sure to be disgraced, whatever side he took." The Wesleyan emphasis on the moral dilemma and God's preventing grace is clear. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_samuel/29.htm

**The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** Develops the theme "A Good Man in Bad Company," emphasizing David's humiliation (both outwardly before the Philistines and inwardly before God), and the "Illustration of Divine Providence" — "Often a man's enemies open to him the way out of great difficulty." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/29.htm

### Plymouth Brethren

**Grant's Commentary:** Notes the deliberate ambiguity in David's phrase "my lord the king" — Achish assumed David meant him, but David meant Saul. Grant calls David's protest "deceitful." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-samuel-29.html

---

## Other Views

**The Expositor's Bible Commentary (Blaikie, 19th c.):** Takes a more sympathetic view. Blaikie sees David's decline beginning with distrust, then producing dissimulation. David is brought "into the most painful dilemma, and into experience of the most grievous disaster; but God, in His infinite mercy, extricates him from the one and enables him to retrieve the other." Blaikie praises the "singular, unblemished trustworthiness" that David showed Achish, comparing it to Joseph in Potiphar's house — even amid backsliding, David kept his light shining before men. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-samuel-29.html

**1 Chronicles 12:19–22 (cross-reference noted by Precept Austin and Ellicott):** Provides an important parallel account: "From Manasseh also some defected to David when he was about to go to battle with the Philistines against Saul. But they did not help them, for the lords of the Philistines after consultation sent him away, saying, 'At the cost of our heads he may defect to his master Saul.'" This confirms that David was providentially prevented from fighting. The Chronicles account adds that as David went to Ziklag, men from Manasseh defected to him — mighty men of valor who helped him against the Amalekite raiders. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-29-commentary
